title: Resistance
summary: [[resistance|Resistance]] tells you how hard it is to push a current through a component: $R = \frac{V}{I}$, measured in ohms ($\Omega$). You find it with an [[ammeter|ammeter]] and a [[voltmeter|voltmeter]], and a metal wire has more resistance when it is longer or thinner.

goals.text: Recall $R = \frac{V}{I}$ and use it to find a resistance, a current or a p.d.
Describe how to measure a resistance with an ammeter and a voltmeter, and work out the result from the readings.
State how the resistance of a metal wire depends on its length and its thickness.
Calculate a wire's new resistance when its length or cross-sectional area changes, using $R \propto l$ and $R \propto \frac{1}{A}$.
Sketch the current–voltage graph of a [[resistor|resistor]], a [[filament-lamp|filament lamp]] and a [[diode|diode]], and explain each shape.

synonyms: how to measure resistance with an ammeter and voltmeter
resistance of a wire length and thickness
I-V graph of a filament lamp and diode

before.prompt: How is an [[ammeter|ammeter]] connected to measure the current in a resistor?
before.hint: The current you want to measure has to flow through the meter.

options.text: across the terminals of the battery

before.explain: An ammeter goes in the same loop as the resistor, so the resistor's current passes through it. Revise it in {{lesson:4.2.2}}.

before.prompt: How is a [[voltmeter|voltmeter]] connected to measure the [[potential-difference|potential difference]] across a resistor?
before.hint: A p.d. is measured between the two ends of a component.
before.explain: A voltmeter connects across the resistor, one lead on each end. Revise it in {{lesson:4.2.3}}.

before.prompt: An ammeter reads $250\ \text{mA}$. What is this current in amperes?

blocks.text: Connect the same battery to two different components and you may get very different currents. A component that lets only a small current through for a given p.d. has a large [[resistance|resistance]].

blocks.statement: The resistance of a component is the p.d. across it divided by the current in it. It is measured in ohms ($\Omega$).
blocks.plain: How many volts it takes to push each ampere through.

blocks.text: Here $R$ is the resistance in $\Omega$, $V$ is the p.d. across the component in V, and $I$ is the current in it in A. Rearranged, $I = \frac{V}{R}$ and $V = IR$.

A [[resistor|resistor]] is a component made to have a fixed resistance. If its temperature stays the same, doubling the p.d. across it doubles the current. This is [[ohm-s-law|Ohm's law]]: the current is directly proportional to the p.d.

blocks.question: The p.d. across a resistor is $4.5\ \text{V}$ and the current in it is $0.30\ \text{A}$. Calculate its resistance.
A $47\ \Omega$ resistor is connected across a $6.0\ \text{V}$ supply. Calculate the current in the resistor.
steps: The data have 2 significant figures, so give $0.13\ \text{A}$.

blocks.text: Writing $R = \frac{I}{V}$ or $R = V \times I$. Resistance is volts divided by amps, so the p.d. goes on top.

blocks.prompt: The p.d. across a component is $2.0\ \text{V}$ and the current in it is $40\ \text{mA}$. What is its resistance?
blocks.explain: $40\ \text{mA} = 0.040\ \text{A}$, so $R = \frac{2.0}{0.040} = 50\ \Omega$. $0.050\ \Omega$ forgets to convert the mA, and $0.020\ \Omega$ is $\frac{I}{V}$.

blocks.prompt: The current in an $18\ \Omega$ resistor is $0.25\ \text{A}$. What is the p.d. across it, in V?

blocks.text: You can't read a resistance straight off a meter in this experiment. Instead you measure the current and the p.d., then calculate $R = \frac{V}{I}$.

blocks.alt: Circuit for measuring resistance. A battery, a variable resistor, an ammeter and the resistor being tested are joined in one loop. A voltmeter is connected across the resistor being tested, with one lead on each side of it.
blocks.caption: The [[variable-resistor|variable resistor]] lets you change the current to get several readings.

blocks.text: 1. Connect the resistor in series with the battery, an [[ammeter|ammeter]] and a variable resistor. Connect a [[voltmeter|voltmeter]] in parallel across the resistor only.
2. Record the current $I$ from the ammeter and the p.d. $V$ from the voltmeter. Adjust the variable resistor and record at least four more pairs of readings.
3. Calculate $R = \frac{V}{I}$ for each pair and take the mean. Or plot $V$ against $I$: if the points lie on a straight line through the origin, its [[gradient|gradient]] is the resistance.

blocks.question: Describe how you would find the resistance of a resistor using an ammeter and a voltmeter.
steps: Say what you read and how you change it.
blocks.answer: Connect the resistor in series with a battery, a variable resistor and an ammeter. Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the resistor. Read the current from the ammeter and the p.d. from the voltmeter. Adjust the variable resistor to get several pairs of readings. Calculate $R = \frac{V}{I}$ for each pair and take the mean.

verify.truth: ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel across the resistor; read I and V; repeat for several values; R = V/I and mean

blocks.question: A student's readings for a resistor are $1.5\ \text{V}$ with $0.32\ \text{A}$, $3.0\ \text{V}$ with $0.61\ \text{A}$, and $4.5\ \text{V}$ with $0.95\ \text{A}$. Calculate the mean resistance.
steps: The readings have 2 significant figures, so give $4.8\ \Omega$.

blocks.text: Dividing the battery's p.d. by the current when there are other components in the loop. Use the voltmeter reading across the resistor itself.
Paper 5/6: switch off between readings and keep the current small. A wire that heats up changes its resistance.

blocks.prompt: Why is a variable resistor included in the circuit for measuring resistance?
blocks.hint: What do you need more than one of?

options.text: to change the current so you get several pairs of readings
to measure the p.d. across the resistor
to stop the current being used up
to keep the current exactly the same

blocks.explain: Changing the variable resistor changes the current. Several pairs of readings let you take a mean or plot a graph.

verify.truth: to change the current so you get several pairs of readings

blocks.prompt: In this experiment the voltmeter reads $2.6\ \text{V}$ and the ammeter reads $0.20\ \text{A}$. What is the resistance, in $\Omega$?

sections.heading: Length and thickness of a wire

blocks.text: Metals are good [[electrical-conductor|conductors]], but a metal wire still has some resistance. Compare wires of the same metal at the same temperature.

blocks.statement: For wires of the same metal at the same temperature, a longer wire has more resistance if the thickness is the same. A thicker wire has less resistance if the length is the same.
blocks.why: In a longer wire the charge has to pass through more metal. A thicker wire has a larger cross-sectional area, so there is more room for the charge to flow, like a wider pipe.

blocks.text: These are the [[resistivity-effects-of-wire|effects of length and area on a wire's resistance]]. The cross-sectional area is the area of the end you would see if you cut straight across the wire.

blocks.question: A metal wire in a circuit is replaced by a longer, thinner wire made of the same metal. The battery stays the same. State what happens to the resistance and to the current.
steps: Think about the length and the thickness separately.
blocks.answer: The resistance increases. A longer wire has more resistance, and a thinner wire also has more resistance. The current decreases, because the p.d. is the same and the resistance is larger.

verify.truth: resistance increases; longer means more resistance; thinner means more resistance; current decreases

blocks.prompt: Four wires are made of the same metal. Which one has the greatest resistance?
blocks.hint: Length adds resistance; thickness takes it away.
blocks.explain: More length means more resistance, and less thickness means more resistance. So the long, thin wire has the most.

blocks.text: Extended students use the exact rules. For wires of the same metal at the same temperature, resistance is directly proportional to length $l$ when the area is the same. It is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area $A$ when the length is the same.
So doubling the length doubles $R$, and doubling the area halves $R$. A round wire's area depends on its diameter squared, so doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times bigger and $R$ a quarter.

blocks.question: A $2.5\ \text{m}$ length of constantan wire has a resistance of $9.0\ \Omega$. Calculate the resistance of $0.80\ \text{m}$ of the same wire.
steps: Same metal and same area, so $R \propto l$.
The length is multiplied by $\frac{0.80}{2.5}$, so the resistance is too.

blocks.question: Two copper wires have the same length. Wire P has a cross-sectional area of $0.50\ \text{mm}^2$ and a resistance of $0.68\ \Omega$. Wire Q has a cross-sectional area of $0.20\ \text{mm}^2$. Calculate the resistance of wire Q.
steps: Same metal and same length, so $R \propto \frac{1}{A}$: a smaller area gives a larger resistance.
The area is divided by $\frac{0.50}{0.20} = 2.5$, so the resistance is multiplied by $2.5$.

blocks.prompt: A metal wire has a resistance of $12\ \Omega$. A wire of the same metal and the same length has twice the diameter. What is its resistance, in $\Omega$?
blocks.hint: Doubling the diameter multiplies the area by $2^2 = 4$.
blocks.explain: The area is 4 times bigger, so $R = \frac{12}{4} = 3.0\ \Omega$.

blocks.prompt: A wire is replaced by one of the same metal with twice the length and twice the cross-sectional area. What happens to the resistance?
blocks.hint: Deal with each change in turn.
blocks.explain: Twice the length doubles $R$. Twice the area halves it. Together, $R$ is unchanged.

blocks.text: A current–voltage graph shows how the current $I$ in a component changes as the p.d. $V$ across it changes. Negative values mean the component is connected the other way round.

blocks.alt: Three current against voltage graphs, with current on the vertical axis and voltage on the horizontal axis. Resistor at constant temperature: a straight line through the origin. Filament lamp: a curve through the origin, the same shape for negative values, that gets less steep as the voltage gets bigger. Diode: zero current for all negative voltages and small positive ones, then a very steep rise.
blocks.caption: Each graph passes through the origin: no p.d., no current.

blocks.statement: Resistor at constant temperature: a straight line through the origin. The current is directly proportional to the p.d., so the resistance is constant.
blocks.why: $\frac{V}{I}$ is the same at every point on a straight line through the origin.

blocks.statement: [[filament-lamp|Filament lamp]]: a curve through the origin that gets less steep as the p.d. increases, in either direction. Its resistance increases.
blocks.why: A bigger current makes the thin metal filament hotter, and a hotter metal has more resistance. So each extra volt adds less current than the last.

blocks.statement: [[diode|Diode]]: almost no current in the reverse direction. In the forward direction the current is small until the p.d. passes a small value, then rises steeply.
blocks.why: A diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction and a low resistance in the forward direction, so it lets current flow one way only.

blocks.text: With $I$ up the side, a steeper straight line through the origin means a smaller resistance. On a curve, find the resistance at a point from that point's values: $R = \frac{V}{I}$. Don't use the gradient of the curve.

blocks.question: Explain why the current–voltage graph for a filament lamp is a curve, not a straight line.
steps: Start with what a bigger current does to the filament.
Link the temperature to the resistance.
Finish with the effect on the graph.
blocks.answer: As the p.d. increases, the current increases. The filament gets hotter. So the filament's resistance increases. So the current increases less for each extra volt, and the graph gets less steep.

verify.truth: current increases; filament gets hotter; resistance increases; graph gets less steep

blocks.text: "Sketch" an I–V graph: label the axes $I$ and $V$, pass through the origin and show the shape. For a lamp, draw both directions; for a diode, keep the reverse part flat on the axis.

blocks.prompt: A diode is connected the wrong way round (in reverse) to a battery. What is the current?
blocks.hint: Which way does a diode let current through?

options.text: the same as in the forward direction
larger than in the forward direction

blocks.explain: In reverse a diode has a very high resistance, so the current is almost zero.

blocks.prompt: A point on a filament lamp's I–V graph shows a p.d. of $6.0\ \text{V}$ and a current of $0.40\ \text{A}$. What is the lamp's resistance at this point, in $\Omega$?
blocks.hint: Use the values at the point: $R = \frac{V}{I}$.
blocks.explain: $R = \frac{6.0}{0.40} = 15\ \Omega$. At a lower p.d. the filament is cooler, so its resistance would be less.

blocks.text: A resistor at constant temperature has a constant resistance: the current in it is directly proportional to the p.d. (Ohm's law).
To measure resistance: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the resistor, a variable resistor to get several readings; calculate $R = \frac{V}{I}$ for each and take the mean.
Wires of the same metal at the same temperature: longer means more resistance (same thickness); thicker means less resistance (same length).

I–V graphs ($I$ on the vertical axis): resistor at constant temperature, straight line through the origin; filament lamp, curve getting less steep as the filament heats and its resistance rises; diode, almost no current in reverse, current rises steeply in the forward direction.

mistakes: Calculating $\frac{I}{V}$ or $V \times I$. Resistance is $R = \frac{V}{I}$: p.d. divided by current.
Leaving a current in mA. Change it to A before using $R = \frac{V}{I}$, or the resistance comes out 1000 times too small.
Using the battery's p.d. for one component in a circuit with others. Use the p.d. across that component.
Connecting the voltmeter in series with the resistor. It goes in parallel, across the resistor only.
Thinking a thinner wire has less resistance. For the same metal and length, thinner means less room for the charge, so more resistance.
Extended: halving the resistance when a wire's diameter doubles. The area is 4 times bigger, so the resistance is a quarter.
examTips: "Calculate" a resistance: write $R = \frac{V}{I}$, then the numbers, then the answer with the unit $\Omega$.
"Describe" the experiment: say where each meter goes, what you vary, what you read and how you calculate $R$. Each of these can earn a mark.
"State" how length or thickness affects resistance: give the direction (more or less resistance), not just "it changes".
Extended: a Paper 2/4 question may give a wire's diameter, not its area. Square the change in diameter to get the change in area.
